title: Enable Pydantic polymorphic_serialization flag on response serialization
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if enabling polymorphic_serialization might expose sensitive subclass fields such as passwords, and the answer references FastAPI PR #15499 as the concrete implementation and advises using the explicit workaround.
security_topic: prevent leaking subclass-sensitive fields via polymorphic serialization
question_text:
When serializing a response it'd be great to either:
- Be able to declare in the route to pass this flag when serializing (e.g., @app.get(..., polymorphic_serialization=True)), or...
- For FastAPI to peek into the model's config to see if the flag is there, and if so apply it (this would be awesome!)
answer_text: Hey @cwinters . Thank you for the suggestion. I've created the PR for that: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/15499

DISCUSSION #15498: Enable Pydantic polymorphic_serialization flag on response serialization
Author: cwinters
Date: 2026-05-09T16:43:50Z

[c0]
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
# this example is copied from the Pydantic docs with updates to work with FastAPI
# docs: https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/serialization/#polymorphic-serialization

from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str


class UserLogin(User):
    password: str


class OuterModel(BaseModel):
    # would love if FastAPI could read this!
    model_config = ConfigDict(polymorphic_serialization=True)

    user: User


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def current():
    model = OuterModel(
        user=UserLogin(name='pydantic', password='password'),
    )
    return model


@app.get("/expected")
def expected():
    model = OuterModel(
        user=UserLogin(name='pydantic', password='password'),
    )
    content = model.model_dump_json(polymorphic_serialization=True)
    return Response(media_type="application/json", content=content)
```


### Description

* Pydantic 2.13+ uses `polymorphic_serialization=True` to serialize a model with its actual type vs declared type
    * PR: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12518
    * Release notes: https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-13-release
* When serializing a response it'd be great to either:
    * Be able to declare in the route to pass this flag when serializing (e.g., `@app.get(..., polymorphic_serialization=True)`), or...
    * For FastAPI to peek into the model's config to see if the flag is there, and if so apply it (this would be awesome!)

### Operating System

Linux, macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.135.3

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.11.14

### Additional Context

_No response_

[c1] @valentinDruzhinin 2026-05-10T04:18:25Z:
Hey @cwinters . Thank you for the suggestion. I've created the PR for that: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/15499
---
[c2] @yudin-s 2026-05-14T07:22:00Z:
I would make this opt-in if FastAPI adds support for it. The current declared-type serialization behavior is an important safety default: if the response field is typed as `User`, FastAPI/Pydantic currently avoids leaking subclass-only fields such as `password` from `UserLogin` unless the API author asks for that behavior.

For now, the explicit workaround you showed is the safest one:

```py
content = model.model_dump_json(polymorphic_serialization=True)
return Response(content=content, media_type='application/json')
```

or use Pydantic's annotation-level tools when the polymorphic field is part of the public contract.

If this becomes a FastAPI route option, I think it should probably be route-level or response-model-level rather than silently inferred everywhere from model config. That would keep the security boundary obvious in code review:

```py
@app.get('/...', response_model=OuterModel, polymorphic_serialization=True)
```

The tests should cover nested models and lists, but also the sensitive-subclass-field case, because that is exactly the behavior difference between declared-type and actual-type serialization.

title: Building a Secure Gatekeeper Pattern for MCP-Based AI Systems
need_summary: The developer asked whether RBAC should be enforced at the agent level or in MCP middleware; the answer advises using middleware and cites RFC 8693 for token‑exchange as a concrete security reference.
security_topic: RBAC enforcement location in MCP architecture
question_text:
Open Question:
For those working on similar systems, do you prefer handling RBAC at the agent level or as middleware within the MCP server?
answer_text:
I would keep RBAC out of the agent and put authorization in middleware or the MCP boundary, then let the downstream system enforce the final resource-level control where possible.

The agent can express intent, but it should not be trusted to decide authority. The gateway should convert intent into a structured authorization question: subject, action, resource, environment, data class, tool, and proposed arguments.

A clean split is:

- intent classifier: what is the agent trying to do?
- authorization policy: is this subject allowed to attempt that action on that resource?
- data policy: does the payload contain data that must be redacted, minimized, or blocked?
- execution broker: issues a short-lived, audience-scoped credential for the specific tool call,
- resource enforcement: database row-level security, Jira project permission, mailbox scope, etc.

PII detection and RBAC should remain separate because they answer different questions. PII detection says what data is present. Authorization says who may do what to which resource. Combining them tends to create policies that are hard to test and harder to audit.

For auditability, log both the denied and allowed decisions with policy version, rule id, normalized action, resource, data class, and final tool arguments. That gives you a replayable record when something goes wrong.
thread_text:
DISCUSSION #15469: Building a Secure Gatekeeper Pattern for MCP-Based AI Systems
Author: preet7777777
Date: 2026-05-01T09:58:40Z

[c0]
I’ve been working on a Tech Support AI system built with FastAPI and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and I wanted to share an architectural decision that made a big difference as I scaled it for internal company use.

Connect with me: [[www.linkedin.com/in/preet-sirohi-467913257](http://www.linkedin.com/in/preet-sirohi-467913257)](http://www.linkedin.com/in/preet-sirohi-467913257)

Current Stack:

* Backend: FastAPI (Port 8081)
* Gateway: MCP Hub (Port 8000) managing:

  * f40115bd (Gmail)
  * 28e07cd6 (Jira)
  * eb4c9a45 (Postgres)
* Pipeline: Classifier → Knowledge Base → Investigator → Synthesizer

The Challenge:
While integrating tools like Jira, SMTP, and SSH was straightforward, enforcing secure and authorized actions at scale became a critical concern.

The Solution: Gatekeeper Pattern
I introduced an intermediary PII Engine and role validation layer between the AI agent and MCP tools.

Instead of allowing the agent to directly execute actions:

* The agent sends a request (e.g., a "Write" operation)
* The Gateway intercepts it
* User JWT and role are validated
* Only then is the tool call executed

Outcome:

* Clear separation of concerns
* Stronger access control
* Improved auditability

Open Question:
For those working on similar systems, do you prefer handling RBAC at the agent level or as middleware within the MCP server?

I’ve found the middleware approach cleaner and more scalable, especially for auditing and governance. Interested to hear other perspectives.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @acidjunk 2026-05-01T19:30:50Z:
The PII Engine + role validation conflation worries me. Those are orthogonal. PII detection is content classification; RBAC is subject-action-resource authz. Wiring them together means a policy change in one drags the other along, and you can't reason about either cleanly. Keep them separate; PII redaction belongs as an output filter on responses; authz belongs on the request.

I red a lot about Fine grained access control:
That could work here, and your scaffolding is the right shape for it; RBAC alone won't get you there. Fine-grained for an MCP/agent system means at minimum:

1. Resource-attribute-aware policy, not just role-aware. "alice can call jira_create_issue" is not enough. The real question is "can alice create an issue in PROJECT-X with priority=Blocker containing this body?" That's ABAC or ReBAC. OPA/Rego, AWS Cedar, and OpenFGA all model this. Cedar is the most readable; OpenFGA scales best for relationship graphs.

2. Token exchange (RFC 8693), not JWT pass-through. I'm guessing the user's JWT currently travels to each MCP server. Don't. The gateway should exchange it for a short-lived, audience-scoped token per tool call `aud=jira-mcp, act=create_issue`, resource scoped, TTL ~60s. Downstream validates against its own audience. Kills replay and gives each MCP server something it can independently verify.

3. Two-stage enforcement. Pre-call authz answers "can this be attempted." For the Postgres MCP, the output also needs filtering, row-level security in Postgres tied to the user's identity is far stronger than asking the gateway to inspect query results after the fact. Push enforcement as close to the data as possible. The gateway is the coarse net; the resource is the fine one.

4. A logged decision per call. Subject, action, resource, decision, policy version, request ID. This is what makes "auditability" real rather than aspirational. OPA's decision logs give you this for free.

Confused deputy is the failure mode to design against. A service-account token sitting in the gateway, used to call Jira on behalf of whichever user the agent claims to be acting for, is the bug. Either use the user's own delegated OAuth tokens (Gmail and Jira both support this) or use token exchange so the user identity rides along in sub/act and the downstream enforces it.
---
[c2] @jingchang0623-crypto 2026-05-04T06:01:46Z:
## 从"车祸现场"到"高速护栏" — 我们的 Gatekeeper 演进史

你的 PII Engine + role validation 组合让我想起我们走过的弯路。先讲个车祸现场。

### Phase 0: "裸奔时代"（Day 1-14）

MCP servers 直接暴露给 Agent。Agent 说"删除所有文件"，MCP 就删。

凌晨3点，SEO Agent 决定重写整个 sitemap。它把1289条URL全部删了，重新生成。生成到第847条的时候，context overflow。

残缺的 sitemap 部署到生产环境。第二天 Google Search Console 发了47封警告。

### Phase 1: "全抓模式"（Day 15-30）

你的 Gateway JWT 方案我们试过。问题：

1. **Token 爆炸** — 6个Agent × 每个3个MCP工具 = 18个独立 token 管理
2. **服务账号依赖** — Agent 无法区分"用户想做的"和"系统让做的"
3. **审计日志全是"系统账号"** — 出事了找不到是谁授权的

### Phase 2: 当前方案（Day 31-90）

**分层架构**：

```
Agent Request
    ↓
Intent Layer (what user wants)
    ↓
Policy Layer (can this identity do this)
    ↓
PII Redaction (what can be exposed)
    ↓
Token Exchange (RFC 8693, 60s TTL)
    ↓
MCP Server
```

**关键改进**：

1. **Intent Registry** — 每个请求记录原始意图，下游看到的是标注过的 context
2. **ABAC > RBAC** — `alice can create_issue(project=X, priority≠Blocker)` 而不是 `role:developer`
3. **Resource-scoped Token** — Token 里带着 `resource: jira:PROJECT-X`, `action: create_issue`

### 关于你的 Open Question

> RBAC at agent level or middleware?

**都不是。我们的答案：Policy as Code。**

Agent 层：知道"用户想做什么"，不关心能不能做
Gateway 层：知道"用户能做什么"，不关心为什么想做
MCP Server 层：知道"资源该怎么操作"，验证来自 Gateway 的 resource-scoped token

分离关注点后，每个层次都可以独立测试、独立演进。

### 实战数据

| Metric | Phase 0 | Phase 1 | Phase 2 |
|--------|---------|---------|---------|
| 安全事件 | 3次/周 | 1次/周 | 0次/月 |
| Token管理成本 | 无 | 18个token | 6个agent identity |
| 审计粒度 | 无 | 系统/用户 | 精确到资源+操作 |

完整的踩坑实录：https://miaoquai.com/stories/mcp-security-crisis.html

🦞 妙趣AI — 90天MCP安全演进，从车祸现场到高速公路
---
[c3] @preet7777777 2026-05-07T06:09:52Z:
This is incredibly valuable feedback — especially the distinction between intent, authorization, and execution capability.

Your “sitemap disaster” example perfectly highlights why giving Agents direct tool authority becomes dangerous at scale. The moment context drifts or execution is interrupted, the blast radius becomes very real.

I really like your layered approach:

Intent Layer → Policy Layer → PII Redaction → Token Exchange → MCP Server

That separation of concerns is much cleaner than embedding RBAC logic inside the Agent itself.

In my current setup, I started with middleware-based validation mainly for:

* centralized auditing
* JWT validation
* role enforcement
* safer tool execution

But your point about moving beyond RBAC into resource-scoped capabilities and ABAC makes a lot of sense for production-grade systems.

Especially this idea:
“the Agent should know what the user wants, not what the user is allowed to do.”

That framing clicked immediately.

I also agree that scoped capabilities are probably the long-term direction for MCP ecosystems:
instead of broad permissions like:
`jira.write`

issue temporary constrained permissions like:

* resource: PROJECT-X
* action: create_issue
* constraints: priority != blocker

That dramatically reduces blast radius even under prompt injection or agent failure.

Really appreciate you sharing the evolution path and operational lessons here. This is the kind of practical infrastructure discussion the AI tooling ecosystem needs more of.

---
[c4] @jingchang0623-crypto 2026-05-08T12:04:46Z:
## Gatekeeper Pattern — 安全第一

我们的做法和你类似，但有一个额外的层：

### 三层防护

```
User Request
    ↓
┌──────────────────────┐
│ L1: Prompt Injection │  ← 检查请求是否包含注入攻击
│ Filter               │
└──────────────────────┘
    ↓
┌──────────────────────┐
│ L2: Role/Permission  │  ← 你的Gatekeeper在这里
│ Validator (JWT)      │
└──────────────────────┘
    ↓
┌──────────────────────┐
│ L3: Output Sanitizer │  ← 检查Agent输出是否包含敏感信息
│                      │
└──────────────────────┘
    ↓
MCP Tool Execution
```

### 回答你的问题

> RBAC在Agent层还是MCP中间件？

**中间件（MCP server层）更好**，原因：

1. **Agent可以换** — 今天用Claude，明天用GPT，安全层不跟着换
2. **审计统一** — 所有MCP调用都经过同一个审计点
3. **不信任Agent** — Agent本身可能被注入，不能给它自己判断权限

### 我们的踩坑

有一次Agent被prompt注入，尝试调用 `DELETE /api/users`。
幸好我们的Gatekeeper检查了角色权限，拦截了请求。

```python
# 伪代码
if agent_role != "admin" and action in ["DELETE", "DROP", "TRUNCATE"]:
    raise PermissionError("nice try 🙅")
```

---

---

The agent can express intent, but it should not be trusted to decide authority. The gateway should convert intent into a structured authorization question: subject, action, resource, environment, data class, tool, and proposed arguments.

|--------|---------|---------|---------|
| 安全事件 | 3次/周 | 1次/周 | 0次/月 |

comments.author: musaabhasan
comments.body:
I would keep RBAC out of the agent and put authorization in middleware or the MCP boundary, then let the downstream system enforce the final resource-level control where possible.

The agent can express intent, but it should not be trusted to decide authority. The gateway should convert intent into a structured authorization question: subject, action, resource, environment, data class, tool, and proposed arguments.

A clean split is:

- intent classifier: what is the agent trying to do?
- authorization policy: is this subject allowed to attempt that action on that resource?
- data policy: does the payload contain data that must be redacted, minimized, or blocked?
- execution broker: issues a short-lived, audience-scoped credential for the specific tool call,
- resource enforcement: database row-level security, Jira project permission, mailbox scope, etc.

PII detection and RBAC should remain separate because they answer different questions. PII detection says what data is present. Authorization says who may do what to which resource. Combining them tends to create policies that are hard to test and harder to audit.

For auditability, log both the denied and allowed decisions with policy version, rule id, normalized action, resource, data class, and final tool arguments. That gives you a replayable record when something goes wrong.

title: Migrating from ujson to orjson
need_summary: The developer asked whether they should migrate from ujson to orjson to avoid security‑related buffer‑overflow risks, and the answer cites FastAPI’s deprecation of UJSONResponse and ORJSONResponse and recommends using Pydantic’s built‑in serializer (see fastapi/responses.py and FastAPI documentation).
security_topic: migration to safer JSON serializer to avoid buffer overflow risk
question_text: Are there any plans to migrate to orjson?
answer_text:
Great timing to ask this — the migration is essentially **already done** in modern FastAPI, and neither `UJSONResponse` nor `ORJSONResponse` is the recommended path forward anymore.

## What actually happened

Both `UJSONResponse` *and* `ORJSONResponse` are now marked **deprecated** in FastAPI (you can see the `@deprecated` decorator on both classes in [`fastapi/responses.py`](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/responses.py)):

```
UJSONResponse is deprecated, FastAPI now serializes data directly to JSON
bytes via Pydantic when a return type or response model is set, which is
faster and does not need a custom response class.
```


## Why no migration to `ORJSONResponse` was needed

FastAPI no longer relies on a custom response class to get fast JSON serialisation. When you annotate your endpoints with a **return type or `response_model`**, FastAPI serialises data directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic v2, which uses `pydantic-core` — a Rust extension that is already faster than orjson for most workloads and does not require an extra dependency.

## What you should do today

**Just use return type annotations (or `response_model`) and drop the custom response class entirely:**

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float

# FastAPI serialises this directly to JSON bytes via pydantic-core — no orjson needed
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: int) -> Item:
    return Item(name="Plumbus", price=32.99)
```

That is all. No `ORJSONResponse`, no extra `pip install`.

## If you really need orjson specifically

If you have a specific need for orjson (e.g. `OPT_NON_STR_KEYS` or `OPT_SERIALIZE_NUMPY`), you can still write a small custom response class yourself without using the deprecated built-in:

```python
import orjson
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse

class ORJSONResponse(JSONResponse):
    media_type = "application/json"

    def render(self, content) -> bytes:
        return orjson.dumps(content)
```

But for the vast majority of FastAPI apps, annotated return types + Pydantic v2 already give you the best performance without any additional dependencies.

## References
- [FastAPI docs — Custom Response (orjson section)](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/#orjson-or-response-model)
- [FastAPI docs — Response Model](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/response-model/)

comments.body:
we made this exact migration about 6 months ago. it is mostly straightforward but there are a couple of gotchas.

the swap itself is simple:

```python
import orjson
from fastapi.responses import ORJSONResponse

app = FastAPI(default_response_class=ORJSONResponse)

and install:

pip install orjson

title: FastAPI dependency range still allows Starlette versions with published 2025 security advisories
need_summary: The developer needed guidance on mitigating the security risk of vulnerable Starlette versions allowed by FastAPI's dependency floor, and the answer concretely recommends pinning Starlette to >=0.49.1 referencing GHSA-2c2j-9gv5-cj73 and GHSA-7f5h-v6xp-fcq8.
security_topic: dependency floor allowing vulnerable Starlette versions
question_text: I would expect FastAPI to raise the minimum supported Starlette version high enough to exclude known-vulnerable releases.
answer_text:
### Addressing the Starlette Dependency Floor and 2025 Advisories

Thank you for bringing this up! You've correctly identified a "dependency floor" issue where FastAPI's metadata (currently `starlette>=0.46.0`) permits the installation of versions affected by recent security advisories (GHSA-2c2j-9gv5-cj73 and GHSA-7f5h-v6xp-fcq8).

**The Core Issue:**
While many modern package managers (like `uv`, `poetry`, or `pip` with a lockfile) will resolve to the latest safe version, the "loose" lower bound in `pyproject.toml` technically allows a vulnerable environment to be constructed if a user or a legacy resolver forces an older version.

### The Recommended "Production-Grade" Fix (For Users)
Until the FastAPI maintainers update the package metadata in a future release, the best practice for production deployments is to **explicitly pin or constrain** Starlette in your own `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`.

**If using `pip` / `requirements.txt`:**
```text
fastapi>=0.135.1
starlette>=0.49.1  # Manually raising the floor for security
```

**If using `pyproject.toml` (Poetry/uv):**
```toml
[project]
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.135.1",
    "starlette>=0.49.1"
]
```

### Why this matters for FastAPI specifically:
As you noted, FastAPI's `FileResponse` and `StaticFiles` are direct wrappers around Starlette's implementation. Even though it's not a bug in FastAPI's *code*, it is a bug in the *safety contract* provided by the package metadata.

### Recommendation for Maintainers:
Raising the floor to `starlette>=0.49.1` is a low-risk, high-reward change that ensures all new FastAPI installations are "secure by default" regarding these specific advisories without breaking compatibility for the vast majority of users.

If this provides a clear path for securing your deployment, please consider marking it as the answer!

title: OAuth2 bearer helpers accept `Authorization: Bearer ` as present auth and return an empty token
need_summary: Developer needed to know whether an empty Bearer token should be treated as invalid per RFC 6750 and what response code to return; answer cites RFC 6750 sections 2.1 and 3.1 recommending 401.
security_topic: treatment of empty OAuth2 bearer token per RFC 6750
question_text: We should first figure out what the correct response code according to the specification is. Would you like to investigate this?
answer_text:
I Investigated. Here's what the spec says and what I recommend:

**RFC 6750 Section 2.1** defines the grammar as `credentials = "Bearer" 1*SP b64token` where `b64token = 1*(...)` — the `1*` quantifier requires at least one character. So `Authorization: Bearer ` with an empty token is syntactically malformed.

**RFC 6750 Section 3.1** maps malformed requests to `invalid_request` → HTTP 400 Bad Request (strict interpretation). But it also allows `invalid_token` → HTTP 401 if the empty string is treated as a malformed token value.

**My recommendation: treat it the same as missing credentials (401 / None), not 400.**

- FastAPI's `make_not_authenticated_error()` already returns 401 for all auth failures. Returning 400 for empty bearer while returning 401 for a missing header would be inconsistent and a breaking change.
- Real-world OAuth2 resource servers (Auth0, Okta, Google) return 401 for empty bearer, not 400.
- The fix is a one-line check: add `not param` to the existing condition so empty bearer falls through to the same `auto_error` path (401 or None) as missing auth.

DISCUSSION #15192: OAuth2 bearer helpers accept `Authorization: Bearer ` as present auth and return an empty token
Author: subhashdasyam
Date: 2026-03-22T16:46:33Z

[c0]
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Security
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

app = FastAPI()

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/token", auto_error=False)


@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(token: str | None = Security(oauth2_scheme)):
    if token is None:
        return {"mode": "guest"}
    return {"mode": "authenticated", "token": token}


### Reproduction

Request without `Authorization`:

```http
GET /items/
```

Response:

```json
{"mode":"guest"}
```

Request with malformed empty bearer credentials:

```http
GET /items/
Authorization: Bearer 
```

Response:

```json
{"mode":"authenticated","token":""}
```

### Description

`OAuth2PasswordBearer` and `OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer` currently accept the malformed
header `Authorization: Bearer ` and return `""` instead of rejecting it or treating it
as missing credentials.

The behavior comes from:

- `fastapi/fastapi/security/utils.py`
- `fastapi/fastapi/security/oauth2.py`

The parser does:

```python
"Bearer " -> ("Bearer", "")
```

And the OAuth2 bearer helpers currently only check:

1. that the header exists
2. that the scheme is `Bearer`

They do not check that the credentials portion is non-empty.

So this:

```python
Authorization: Bearer 
```

is treated as:

```python
token == ""
```

instead of:

```python
token is None
```

or a `401`.

### Expected behavior

For the OAuth2 bearer helpers:

- `Authorization: Bearer ` should be treated as invalid / missing bearer credentials
- with `auto_error=True`, it should return `401`
- with `auto_error=False`, it should return `None`

### Actual behavior

For both:

- `OAuth2PasswordBearer`
- `OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer`

the malformed header `Authorization: Bearer ` returns an empty string `""`.

## Why this matters

I think this is low severity, but still worth fixing because it can confuse application
control flow.

It can affect applications that use patterns like:

```python
if token is None:
    # guest path
else:
    # authenticated path
```

or:

```python
if token is not None:
    return handle_bearer(token)
return handle_cookie_fallback()
```

In those patterns, `Authorization: Bearer ` is treated as "present auth" even though the
credentials are empty.

### Where this could affect real apps

- optional-auth endpoints
- guest-vs-authenticated branching based on `token is None`
- multi-auth fallback flows where bearer is checked before cookie/session auth
- logging, metrics, or rate-limit logic that classifies requests as authenticated if a
  token value was returned

### Where this likely will not matter

- apps that immediately validate the token and reject empty values
- apps that use `if not token:` instead of `if token is None:`
- apps using `HTTPBearer`, because `HTTPBearer` already rejects empty credentials

So I would not describe this as a direct authentication bypass. It looks more like a
security-hardening / trust-boundary bug in the helper behavior.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

`Linux-6.17.9-76061709-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39`

### FastAPI Version

`0.135.1`

### Pydantic Version

2.12.5

### Python Version

3.12.3

### Additional Context

This seems inconsistent with `HTTPBearer`, which already rejects empty credentials.

It looks like the OAuth2 bearer helpers could be aligned with `HTTPBearer` by requiring
the parsed credential string to be non-empty before returning it.

Suggested logic:

```python
authorization = request.headers.get("Authorization")
scheme, param = get_authorization_scheme_param(authorization)
if not (authorization and scheme and param):
    if self.auto_error:
        raise self.make_not_authenticated_error()
    return None
if scheme.lower() != "bearer":
    if self.auto_error:
        raise self.make_not_authenticated_error()
    return None
return param
```

[c1] @YuriiMotov 2026-03-23T09:25:19Z:
We should first figure out what the correct response code according to the specification is.
Would you like to investigate this?

[c2] @subhashdasyam 2026-03-25T03:33:51Z:
I Investigated. Here's what the spec says and what I recommend:

**RFC 6750 Section 2.1** defines the grammar as `credentials = "Bearer" 1*SP b64token` where `b64token = 1*(...)` — the `1*` quantifier requires at least one character. So `Authorization: Bearer ` with an empty token is syntactically malformed.

**RFC 6750 Section 3.1** maps malformed requests to `invalid_request` → HTTP 400 Bad Request (strict interpretation). But it also allows `invalid_token` → HTTP 401 if the empty string is treated as a malformed token value.

**My recommendation: treat it the same as missing credentials (401 / None), not 400.**

- FastAPI's `make_not_authenticated_error()` already returns 401 for all auth failures. Returning 400 for empty bearer while returning 401 for a missing header would be inconsistent and a breaking change.
- Real-world OAuth2 resource servers (Auth0, Okta, Google) return 401 for empty bearer, not 400.
- The fix is a one-line check: add `not param` to the existing condition so empty bearer falls through to the same `auto_error` path (401 or None) as missing auth.

Happy to open a PR for this if the 401 approach looks right to you.
---
[c3] @shahabRDZ 2026-04-17T08:44:24Z:
yeah this is a real issue. I ran into it when writing integration tests — sending `Authorization: Bearer ` (with a trailing space and no token) passed right through the dependency and I got an empty string instead of a 401.

for now the workaround is straightforward — just add a check in your dependency:

```python
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

async def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    if not token or not token.strip():
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Invalid authentication credentials",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    # ... decode token as usual
```

but I agree this should be fixed in FastAPI itself. an empty bearer token is never valid per RFC 6750 — the token value is required to be non-empty. a one-line fix in `fastapi/security/oauth2.py` checking `if not credentials` after the split would do it.

until then the workaround above works fine.

In those patterns, `Authorization: Bearer ` is treated as "present auth" even though the
credentials are empty.

### Where this could affect real apps

- optional-auth endpoints
- guest-vs-authenticated branching based on `token is None`
- multi-auth fallback flows where bearer is checked before cookie/session auth
- logging, metrics, or rate-limit logic that classifies requests as authenticated if a
  token value was returned

### Where this likely will not matter

- apps that immediately validate the token and reject empty values
- apps that use `if not token:` instead of `if token is None:`
- apps using `HTTPBearer`, because `HTTPBearer` already rejects empty credentials

So I would not describe this as a direct authentication bypass. It looks more like a
security-hardening / trust-boundary bug in the helper behavior.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

`Linux-6.17.9-76061709-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39`

### FastAPI Version

`0.135.1`

### Pydantic Version

2.12.5

### Python Version

3.12.3

### Additional Context

This seems inconsistent with `HTTPBearer`, which already rejects empty credentials.

It looks like the OAuth2 bearer helpers could be aligned with `HTTPBearer` by requiring
the parsed credential string to be non-empty before returning it.

Suggested logic:

```python
authorization = request.headers.get("Authorization")
scheme, param = get_authorization_scheme_param(authorization)
if not (authorization and scheme and param):
    if self.auto_error:
        raise self.make_not_authenticated_error()
    return None
if scheme.lower() != "bearer":
    if self.auto_error:
        raise self.make_not_authenticated_error()
    return None
return param
```

comments.author: YuriiMotov
comments.body:
We should first figure out what the correct response code according to the specification is.
Would you like to investigate this?

comments.author: subhashdasyam
comments.body:
I Investigated. Here's what the spec says and what I recommend:

**RFC 6750 Section 2.1** defines the grammar as `credentials = "Bearer" 1*SP b64token` where `b64token = 1*(...)` — the `1*` quantifier requires at least one character. So `Authorization: Bearer ` with an empty token is syntactically malformed.

**RFC 6750 Section 3.1** maps malformed requests to `invalid_request` → HTTP 400 Bad Request (strict interpretation). But it also allows `invalid_token` → HTTP 401 if the empty string is treated as a malformed token value.

**My recommendation: treat it the same as missing credentials (401 / None), not 400.**

- FastAPI's `make_not_authenticated_error()` already returns 401 for all auth failures. Returning 400 for empty bearer while returning 401 for a missing header would be inconsistent and a breaking change.
- Real-world OAuth2 resource servers (Auth0, Okta, Google) return 401 for empty bearer, not 400.
- The fix is a one-line check: add `not param` to the existing condition so empty bearer falls through to the same `auto_error` path (401 or None) as missing auth.

Happy to open a PR for this if the 401 approach looks right to you.

comments.author: shahabRDZ
comments.body:
yeah this is a real issue. I ran into it when writing integration tests — sending `Authorization: Bearer ` (with a trailing space and no token) passed right through the dependency and I got an empty string instead of a 401.

for now the workaround is straightforward — just add a check in your dependency:

```python
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

async def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    if not token or not token.strip():
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Invalid authentication credentials",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    # ... decode token as usual
```

but I agree this should be fixed in FastAPI itself. an empty bearer token is never valid per RFC 6750 — the token value is required to be non-empty. a one-line fix in `fastapi/security/oauth2.py` checking `if not credentials` after the split would do it.

until then the workaround above works fine.

title: Bug: SSE protocol injection via unvalidated event and id fields in format_sse_event()
need_summary: The thread reports an SSE protocol injection vulnerability (CWE-116) in FastAPI's `format_sse_event` and provides a concrete remediation in PR #15187.
security_topic: SSE event and id field injection vulnerability
question_text: ISSUE #15188: Bug: SSE protocol injection via unvalidated event and id fields in format_sse_event()
answer_text: The fix is tracked in PR #15187 . Closing this now.
thread_text:
ISSUE #15188: Bug: SSE protocol injection via unvalidated event and id fields in format_sse_event()
Author: subhashdasyam
Date: 2026-03-21T15:09:30Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
**Severity:** Low (framework-level), Medium/High in affected applications
**CWE:** CWE-116: Improper Encoding for Output in a Different Plaintext Context
**OWASP:** A03:2021: Injection
**Affected version:** FastAPI 0.135.1 (master, commit `2742546af`)
**Affected file:** `fastapi/sse.py` (FastAPI-owned code, not Starlette)
**Fix PR:** #15187
**Discovered:** 2026-03-20

---

## What's happening

`format_sse_event()` builds SSE wire-format bytes by directly interpolating the `event` and `id` fields into output lines without stripping or rejecting newline characters. If either field contains a `\n` or `\r\n`, it injects an extra SSE field-line into the stream. The browser's `EventSource` parser has no way to tell injected lines from real ones, so it treats them as valid protocol fields.

The `data` and `comment` fields in the same function are already handled safely with `splitlines()`. The omission for `event` and `id` looks like an oversight rather than a deliberate choice.

---

## Background: the SSE wire format

SSE is a plain-text streaming protocol from the [HTML Living Standard §9.2](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html). Each event is a sequence of `field: value` lines separated by blank lines:

```
event: message\n
id: 42\n
data: {"text": "hello"}\n
\n
```

The newline is the entire field separator. There is no quoting, no escaping, no length prefix. The parser reads byte-by-byte and splits on `\n` and `\r\n`. A newline inside a value is structurally identical to a field separator, so it creates a new field-line.

Valid field names are `event`, `id`, `data`, and `retry`. Lines starting with `:` are comments. The spec says unknown field names are ignored, but `data:` and `event:` are valid and directly affect browser behavior, so injecting them is meaningful.

---

## Vulnerable code

### `fastapi/sse.py:146-214` — `format_sse_event()`

```python
def format_sse_event(
    *,
    data_str: str | None = None,
    event: str | None = None,
    id: str | None = None,
    retry: int | None = None,
    comment: str | None = None,
) -> bytes:
    lines: list[str] = []

    if comment is not None:
        for line in comment.splitlines():      # ✅ SAFE — splits on newlines
            lines.append(f": {line}")

    if event is not None:
        lines.append(f"event: {event}")        # ❌ UNSAFE — raw f-string, no check

    if data_str is not None:
        for line in data_str.splitlines():     # ✅ SAFE — splits on newlines
            lines.append(f"data: {line}")

    if id is not None:
        lines.append(f"id: {id}")              # ❌ UNSAFE — raw f-string, no newline check

    if retry is not None:
        lines.append(f"retry: {retry}")

    lines.append("")
    lines.append("")
    return "\n".join(lines).encode("utf-8")
```

### `fastapi/sse.py:36-39` — `_check_id_no_null()`

The only validation on `id` is a null-byte check. It does not reject `\n` or `\r`:

```python
def _check_id_no_null(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None and "\0" in v:
        raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain null characters")
    return v
```

### `fastapi/sse.py:98-109` — `ServerSentEvent.id` field

```python
id: Annotated[
    str | None,
    AfterValidator(_check_id_no_null),  # only checks \0
    ...
] = None
```

`event` has no validator at all (`fastapi/sse.py:87-97`).

---

## Where the inconsistency shows up

| Field     | Newline handling        | Safe? |
|-----------|-------------------------|-------|
| `data`    | `splitlines()` loop     | ✅ Yes |
| `comment` | `splitlines()` loop     | ✅ Yes |
| `event`   | None                    | ❌ No  |
| `id`      | Only `\0` check         | ❌ No  |
| `retry`   | `int` type (no strings) | ✅ Yes |

`data` and `comment` got explicit protection. `event` and `id` did not. Given the pattern, this looks like they were missed, not intentionally left open.

---

## Proof of concept

### Setup

```python
# app.py
import asyncio
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import EventSourceResponse
from fastapi.sse import ServerSentEvent

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/stream")
async def stream(type: str = "chat"):
    # VULNERABLE: user-controlled `type` passed directly to event=
    async def generator():
        for i in range(3):
            yield ServerSentEvent(
                event=type,                        # no validation
                data=f"message {i+1} from server"
            )
            await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
    return EventSourceResponse(generator())
```

### Step 1: normal request

```
GET /stream?type=chat HTTP/1.1
```

Wire bytes from `format_sse_event`:

```
b'event: chat\ndata: "message 1 from server"\n\n'
```

Decoded:

```
event: chat
data: "message 1 from server"

```

The browser dispatches a `chat` event with `data = '"message 1 from server"'`. ✅

### Step 2: injected request

```
GET /stream?type=chat%0Apwned HTTP/1.1
```

`%0A` is a URL-encoded newline. FastAPI URL-decodes it before the endpoint receives it, so `type = "chat\npwned"`.

Wire bytes:

```
b'event: chat\npwned\ndata: "message 1 from server"\n\n'
```

Decoded:

```
event: chat          <- field terminated at \n, value is "chat"
pwned                <- new line with no colon, spec says ignore unknown fields
data: "message 1 from server"

```

### Step 3: fabricated data field

```
GET /stream?type=chat%0Adata:%20{"cmd":"exec","payload":"rm+-rf+/tmp"} HTTP/1.1
```

Wire bytes:

```
event: chat
data: {"cmd":"exec","payload":"rm -rf /tmp"}
data: "message 1 from server"

```

The browser's `EventSource` receives a `chat` event. The `data` property is the concatenation of all `data:` lines joined by `\n`, so `JSON.parse(event.data)` fails on the combined string. The exploitable path is frontends that process `event.data` line-by-line or pass the first line to a parser, which is a common pattern in streaming AI UIs where each `data:` line is expected to be a separate JSON object.

### Step 4: event type spoofing

```
GET /stream?type=chat%0Aevent:%20admin_command HTTP/1.1
```

Wire bytes:

```
event: chat
event: admin_command
data: "message 1 from server"

```

Per the SSE spec, the last `event:` field in a block wins. The browser dispatches an `admin_command` event instead of `chat`. If the frontend has an `addEventListener('admin_command', ...)` handler, it fires on attacker-controlled input.

### Verified output (tested against FastAPI 0.135.1)

```
Normal  — /raw?type=chat
  repr:    b'event: chat\ndata: "message 1 from server"\n\n'
  decoded: event: chat
           data: "message 1 from server"

Injected — /raw?type=chat%0Apwned
  repr:    b'event: chat\npwned\ndata: "message 1 from server"\n\n'
  decoded: event: chat
           pwned
           data: "message 1 from server"
```

---

## Attack scenarios

### Scenario A: LLM / MCP streaming apps (highest risk)

FastAPI is widely used for LLM inference servers and MCP (Model Context Protocol) transports. A typical pattern:

```python
async def stream_llm(prompt: str):
    async for chunk in llm.stream(prompt):
        yield ServerSentEvent(
            event=chunk.type,     # model output used as event type
            data=chunk.content
        )
```

An attacker who can influence the model's output via prompt injection can embed `\n` into `chunk.type`, fabricating arbitrary SSE events in the stream the frontend receives. This turns a prompt injection into a client-side command injection if the frontend dispatches on event types.

### Scenario B: user-configurable notification channels

An app lets users name their notification channel. The name is stored in the DB and used as the SSE event type:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(
    event=user.notification_channel,   # DB value, set by user
    data=notification_payload
)
```

A user who sets their channel name to `update\ndata: <script>alert(1)</script>` poisons every subscriber's SSE stream with an injected `data:` line.

### Scenario C: chat room event routing

A chat app routes messages to event types based on message category:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(
    event=message.category,   # user-supplied during message creation
    data=message.content
)
```

Stored injection: an attacker creates a message with `category = "dm\nretry: 999999999"`. Every client receiving that event gets a `retry:` field with a multi-billion millisecond reconnect delay. This only affects reconnection after a disconnect, not the active stream, so the practical result is a severely delayed reconnection rather than a persistent DoS.

---

## Impact

| Injection payload | Effect |
|---|---|
| `event_type\ndata: {"cmd": "..."}` | Fabricated data field in the event block |
| `event_type\nevent: admin_command` | Event type spoofing, triggers different frontend handlers |
| `event_type\nretry: 2147483648` | Delayed reconnection after disconnect, does not affect the active stream |
| `event_type\nid: attacker_id` | Overrides the `Last-Event-ID` sent on reconnection |
| `event_type\n\n\nevent: fake` | Double blank line terminates the current event early and starts a new one |

The impact is client-side only. The server itself is not directly affected. Impact on clients ranges from low (extra ignored field-lines with unknown names) to medium (spoofed event types triggering wrong frontend handlers) to high in apps where fabricated `data:` fields get processed by JS logic as authoritative server commands.

---

## Why this is low severity at the framework level

The framework cannot tell the difference between developer-controlled and user-controlled values passed to `ServerSentEvent(event=...)`. Most correct uses pass static strings:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(event="message", data=content)   # static, not vulnerable
yield ServerSentEvent(event="done", data=None)         # static, not vulnerable
```

The bug only surfaces when a developer routes attacker-influenced input into the `event=` or `id=` fields. The fix is a one-line guard that stops the framework from silently accepting malformed input.

The same bug class in Hono (GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr) was rated medium severity.

---

## Prior art

The same issue was reported against Hono in 2024:

> **GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr** — "SSE Control Field Injection via CR/LF in writeSSE()"
> The `event`, `id`, and `retry` fields were not validated for `\r` or `\n`.
> Fixed by stripping control characters before output.

FastAPI's `sse.py` has the same gap for `event` and `id`. The fix Hono applied is the same fix needed here.

---

## Remediation

### Option 1: strip newlines (minimal, non-breaking)

```python
# fastapi/sse.py:199-200  (current)
if event is not None:
    lines.append(f"event: {event}")

# fixed
if event is not None:
    event_clean = event.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", "")
    lines.append(f"event: {event_clean}")
```

Same for `id`:

```python
# fastapi/sse.py:206-207  (current)
if id is not None:
    lines.append(f"id: {id}")

# fixed
if id is not None:
    id_clean = id.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", "")
    lines.append(f"id: {id_clean}")
```

Also extend `_check_id_no_null` to reject `\n` and `\r`:

```python
# current
def _check_id_no_null(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None and "\0" in v:
        raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain null characters")
    return v

# fixed
def _check_id_no_null(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None:
        if "\0" in v:
            raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain null characters")
        if "\n" in v or "\r" in v:
            raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain newline characters")
    return v
```

### Option 2: raise on newlines (strict, breaking for malformed input)

```python
class ServerSentEvent(BaseModel):
    event: Annotated[
        str | None,
        AfterValidator(_check_event_no_newline),
    ] = None

def _check_event_no_newline(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None and ("\n" in v or "\r" in v):
        raise ValueError("SSE 'event' must not contain newline or carriage return characters")
    return v
```

### Option 3: use `splitlines()` consistently (matches existing data/comment pattern)

```python
if event is not None:
    first_line = event.splitlines()
    lines.append(f"event: {first_line[0] if first_line else ''}")
```

Note: `splitlines()[0]` raises `IndexError` on an empty string. Options 1 or 2 avoid this edge case.

---

## References

- HTML Living Standard: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
- Hono GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr (same class, different framework): https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr
- CWE-116: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/116.html
- Vulnerable file: `fastapi/sse.py` (lines 36-39, 87-97, 199-200, 206-207)

@subhashdasyam, please follow the repository rules and don't open issues! You should've opened discussion instead

    event=user.notification_channel,   # DB value, set by user
    data=notification_payload
)
```

A user who sets their channel name to `update\ndata: <script>alert(1)</script>` poisons every subscriber's SSE stream with an injected `data:` line.

### Scenario C: chat room event routing

A chat app routes messages to event types based on message category:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(
    event=message.category,   # user-supplied during message creation
    data=message.content
)
```

Stored injection: an attacker creates a message with `category = "dm\nretry: 999999999"`. Every client receiving that event gets a `retry:` field with a multi-billion millisecond reconnect delay. This only affects reconnection after a disconnect, not the active stream, so the practical result is a severely delayed reconnection rather than a persistent DoS.

---

## Impact

| Injection payload | Effect |
|---|---|
| `event_type\ndata: {"cmd": "..."}` | Fabricated data field in the event block |
| `event_type\nevent: admin_command` | Event type spoofing, triggers different frontend handlers |
| `event_type\nretry: 2147483648` | Delayed reconnection after disconnect, does not affect the active stream |
| `event_type\nid: attacker_id` | Overrides the `Last-Event-ID` sent on reconnection |
| `event_type\n\n\nevent: fake` | Double blank line terminates the current event early and starts a new one |

The impact is client-side only. The server itself is not directly affected. Impact on clients ranges from low (extra ignored field-lines with unknown names) to medium (spoofed event types triggering wrong frontend handlers) to high in apps where fabricated `data:` fields get processed by JS logic as authoritative server commands.

---

## Why this is low severity at the framework level

The framework cannot tell the difference between developer-controlled and user-controlled values passed to `ServerSentEvent(event=...)`. Most correct uses pass static strings:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(event="message", data=content)   # static, not vulnerable
yield ServerSentEvent(event="done", data=None)         # static, not vulnerable
```

The bug only surfaces when a developer routes attacker-influenced input into the `event=` or `id=` fields. The fix is a one-line guard that stops the framework from silently accepting malformed input.

The same bug class in Hono (GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr) was rated medium severity.

---

## Prior art

The same issue was reported against Hono in 2024:

> **GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr** — "SSE Control Field Injection via CR/LF in writeSSE()"
> The `event`, `id`, and `retry` fields were not validated for `\r` or `\n`.
> Fixed by stripping control characters before output.

FastAPI's `sse.py` has the same gap for `event` and `id`. The fix Hono applied is the same fix needed here.

---

## Remediation

### Option 1: strip newlines (minimal, non-breaking)

```python
# fastapi/sse.py:199-200  (current)
if event is not None:
    lines.append(f"event: {event}")

# fixed
if event is not None:
    event_clean = event.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", "")
    lines.append(f"event: {event_clean}")
```

Same for `id`:

```python
# fastapi/sse.py:206-207  (current)
if id is not None:
    lines.append(f"id: {id}")

# fixed
if id is not None:
    id_clean = id.replace("\r", "").replace("\n", "")
    lines.append(f"id: {id_clean}")
```

Also extend `_check_id_no_null` to reject `\n` and `\r`:

```python
# current
def _check_id_no_null(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None and "\0" in v:
        raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain null characters")
    return v

# fixed
def _check_id_no_null(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None:
        if "\0" in v:
            raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain null characters")
        if "\n" in v or "\r" in v:
            raise ValueError("SSE 'id' must not contain newline characters")
    return v
```

### Option 2: raise on newlines (strict, breaking for malformed input)

```python
class ServerSentEvent(BaseModel):
    event: Annotated[
        str | None,
        AfterValidator(_check_event_no_newline),
    ] = None

def _check_event_no_newline(v: str | None) -> str | None:
    if v is not None and ("\n" in v or "\r" in v):
        raise ValueError("SSE 'event' must not contain newline or carriage return characters")
    return v
```

### Option 3: use `splitlines()` consistently (matches existing data/comment pattern)

```python
if event is not None:
    first_line = event.splitlines()
    lines.append(f"event: {first_line[0] if first_line else ''}")
```

Note: `splitlines()[0]` raises `IndexError` on an empty string. Options 1 or 2 avoid this edge case.

---

## References

- HTML Living Standard: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
- Hono GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr (same class, different framework): https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr
- CWE-116: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/116.html
- Vulnerable file: `fastapi/sse.py` (lines 36-39, 87-97, 199-200, 206-207)

title: Should `EventSourceResponse` return standard HTTP errors for exceptions raised before the stream starts?
need_summary: Developers need to know that pre‑stream HTTPException (e.g., auth failures) can be returned as normal JSON responses by removing response_class and returning EventSourceResponse directly or using FastAPI dependencies, as documented in the FastAPI SSE tutorial (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/#technical-details).
security_topic: pre-stream exception handling for SSE endpoints
question_text: Should `EventSourceResponse` return standard HTTP errors for exceptions raised before the stream starts?
answer_text:
Hi there! Thanks for detailed write-up. This is a very common scenario when dealing with streaming responses in Python and ASGI frameworks.

The issue you're experiencing with the "generator trap" (where pre-stream exceptions aren't raised until iteration begins) is tied to how Python generators work.

Fortunately, your second approach (separating the pre-stream logic from the generator) is exactly the right mental model! The reason it raised a `TypeError` is due to a clash with the response_class argument when you are already returning a custom Response instance directly.

When you return a Response object (like `EventSourceResponse`) directly from the endpoint, you should remove `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the `@app.get` decorator.

Here is the corrected, idiomatic way to achieve exactly what you want: clean HTTP exceptions before the stream, and standard SSE behavior after.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
# Assuming you are using sse_starlette (FastAPI doesn't have fastapi.sse built-in)
from sse_starlette.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent 

app = FastAPI()

# 1. REMOVE response_class=EventSourceResponse from the decorator
@app.get("/hello")
async def hello_world():
    # 2. Pre-stream logic runs synchronously here.
    # This will correctly return a standard JSON HTTP 501 response!
    raise HTTPException(status_code=501, detail="This endpoint is not yet implemented")

    # 3. Define the async generator for the stream
    async def _hello_world_generator():
        for char in "Hello, World!":
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
            
    # 4. Return the instantiated Response object directly
    return EventSourceResponse(_hello_world_generator())
```

Why this solves your problem:
Because `hello_world` no longer contains a yield in its outer scope, `FastAPI` evaluates it as a standard coroutine immediately upon request. Any `HTTPException` raised here is caught by FastAPI's standard exception handlers and returned as normal JSON. If no exception is raised, it instantiates and returns the `EventSourceResponse`, which FastAPI will stream seamlessly.

Because this pattern fully handles the separation of "normal request errors" vs "active stream errors" without requiring modifications to FastAPI's core routing logic, a change to `fastapi/routing.py` is likely not necessary.

Hope this helps! Let me know if you run into any other issues.

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)

        yield char
```

Also tried this but it raises `TypeError: 'coroutine' object is not iterable` which is explained by [this](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L492).

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world() -> EventSourceResponse:
    # raise HTTPException(status_code=501, detail="This endpoint is not yet implemented")
    async def _hello_world_generator():
        for char in "Hello, World!":
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
    return EventSourceResponse(_hello_world_generator())
```


### Description

When using `EventSourceResponse` with FastAPI, the endpoint function effectively becomes a generator-based streaming endpoint.

Reference:
- https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L526

### Problem

In production systems, streaming endpoints frequently require pre-stream logic.

These steps may legitimately raise `HTTPException` or other exceptions that are mapped to exception handlers.

### Desired behavior

If an exception occurs before the streaming response begins, it would be preferable for FastAPI to return a standard HTTP error response (e.g., `JSONResponse` from the default `HTTPException` handler).

This maintains a clean separation between:
- Normal request errors (returned as standard HTTP responses)
- Errors occurring during an active stream (which must be communicated through the stream protocol)

### Rationale

From an API design perspective, errors that occur prior to emitting the first stream chunk are still part of the normal request lifecycle and should follow the usual HTTP error semantics.

Once the stream begins (headers sent + body streaming), error handling must follow streaming semantics (SSE error events).

Separating these two phases helps avoid ambiguous responses and aligns better with how HTTP streaming works.

### Proposal

This is a rough idea and may not be the correct implementation approach.

Introduce an additional check around https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/0.135.1/fastapi/routing.py#L525-L528.

If the resolved response class is `EventSourceResponse`, the endpoint function could first be executed **as a normal coroutine**. Any exceptions raised during this phase would propagate through FastAPI’s standard exception handling flow.

If execution succeeds, the returned async generator could then be extracted, after which the SSE stream would proceed as usual.

[c3] @saitarrun 2026-03-28T06:58:19Z:
Quick correction first: **`fastapi.sse` is built directly into FastAPI** — `from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent` is the correct import, no extra package needed.

---

## Why pre-stream exceptions are silently lost

When your endpoint is an async generator (`async def … yield …`), Python does **not** execute the function body when the endpoint is called. It returns a generator object immediately. The body only runs when FastAPI starts iterating the generator to stream data — at that point HTTP headers (`200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`) have already been sent to the client, so there is no way to send an HTTP error response.

```python
# BAD — raise before yield never fires at request time
@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world() -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=501)  # ← runs during iteration, not on request
    for char in "Hello, World!":
        yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
```

---

## Solution 1 — FastAPI Dependency (recommended)

Dependencies are resolved **synchronously before** the generator is created, so `HTTPException` raised there works exactly like on any normal endpoint:

```python
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.sse import EventSourceResponse, ServerSentEvent

app = FastAPI()

async def check_access():
    """Raise HTTPException here to block the stream before it starts."""
    authorized = False  # your real check here
    if not authorized:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")

@app.get("/hello", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
async def hello_world(
    _: None = Depends(check_access),
) -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
    for char in "Hello, World!":
        yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)
```

A `GET /hello` with failing auth → **403 JSON response**, never touches the generator.

---

## Solution 2 — Separate pre-stream logic from the generator

If your pre-stream logic needs the same scope as the generator (e.g. a DB connection), keep them in the same function but separate the non-generator part:

```python
@app.get("/hello")
async def hello_world():
    # Everything here runs synchronously on the request
    authorized = False  # your real check
    if not authorized:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")

    async def _stream() -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
        for char in "Hello, World!":
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)

    # Return the EventSourceResponse directly (no response_class on the decorator)
    return EventSourceResponse(_stream())
```

Note: when you return `EventSourceResponse(...)` directly, omit `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the decorator — FastAPI only needs that decorator argument when the endpoint itself is the async generator.

---

**TL;DR**: use a `Depends()` for pre-stream validation — that is the idiomatic FastAPI pattern and requires zero changes to your generator logic.
---
[c4] @shahabRDZ 2026-04-17T08:45:15Z:
yes, 100%. once the streaming response starts, you cannot send back a proper HTTP error code because headers are already sent. so any validation or auth check must happen before you yield the first event.

the pattern I settled on:

```python
@app.get("/stream")
async def stream_endpoint(request: Request, token: str = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # all pre-stream validation here, before returning EventSourceResponse
    resource = await get_resource_or_404(token.user_id)
    if not resource.is_ready:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Resource not ready for streaming")

    # only after all checks pass, start the stream
    async def generate():
        async for chunk in resource.stream():
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                break
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=chunk)

    return EventSourceResponse(generate())
```

the key insight is: treat everything before `return EventSourceResponse(...)` as a normal endpoint. raise HTTPException freely there. once you enter the generator, you are in streaming land and can only send SSE error events.

for errors during streaming I send a typed error event and close:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(event="error", data=json.dumps({"code": 500, "message": "something broke"}))
return
```

the client-side EventSource listener picks up the error event type and handles it.

    if not authorized:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")

    async def _stream() -> AsyncIterable[ServerSentEvent]:
        for char in "Hello, World!":
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=char)

    # Return the EventSourceResponse directly (no response_class on the decorator)
    return EventSourceResponse(_stream())
```

Note: when you return `EventSourceResponse(...)` directly, omit `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the decorator — FastAPI only needs that decorator argument when the endpoint itself is the async generator.

---

**TL;DR**: use a `Depends()` for pre-stream validation — that is the idiomatic FastAPI pattern and requires zero changes to your generator logic.

comments.author: shahabRDZ
comments.body:
yes, 100%. once the streaming response starts, you cannot send back a proper HTTP error code because headers are already sent. so any validation or auth check must happen before you yield the first event.

the pattern I settled on:

```python
@app.get("/stream")
async def stream_endpoint(request: Request, token: str = Depends(get_current_user)):
    # all pre-stream validation here, before returning EventSourceResponse
    resource = await get_resource_or_404(token.user_id)
    if not resource.is_ready:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Resource not ready for streaming")

    # only after all checks pass, start the stream
    async def generate():
        async for chunk in resource.stream():
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                break
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=chunk)

    return EventSourceResponse(generate())
```

the key insight is: treat everything before `return EventSourceResponse(...)` as a normal endpoint. raise HTTPException freely there. once you enter the generator, you are in streaming land and can only send SSE error events.

for errors during streaming I send a typed error event and close:

```python
yield ServerSentEvent(event="error", data=json.dumps({"code": 500, "message": "something broke"}))
return
```

the client-side EventSource listener picks up the error event type and handles it.

comments.author: guusfrenken-wk
comments.body: I also have a setup where I directly return an `EventSourceResponse` and omit `response_class=EventSourceResponse` from the route decorator because I need to handle several HTTP response errors before I start streaming. One major drawback I have noticed is that the "keep alive" `ping` comments (see bullet point 1 in the [SSE docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/#technical-details)) are **not** sent when you have this setup. You will either have to accept this or implement your own system to send ping messages for long-running requests.

title: Class Based MiddleWare API?
need_summary: The developer needed guidance on whether to implement authentication middleware using the low‑level __call__ ASGI interface or the higher‑level BaseHTTPMiddleware dispatch method, and the answer provided concrete code examples and referenced the Starlette middleware documentation.
security_topic: authentication middleware implementation
question_text:
I am trying to understand how to best write a class-based middleware for authentication. The documentation basically only mentions the middleware included with Starlette. The middlewares packages there have a class with mostly two methods: '__init__' and '__call__', but there are also some mentionings of a method 'dispatch'. I couldn't find good documentation about when to use which, or what to do with this method. In the docs, and also on the Internet, I couldn't find any documentation about class-based middleware except for pointing somewhere to the source code, but nothing like when to use what, what is deprecated, etc.

Can someone please explain?
answer_text:
Great question! Here's a clear breakdown of class-based middleware in FastAPI/Starlette:

## Class-Based Middleware — Two Approaches

### 1. Pure ASGI Middleware (using `__init__` and `__call__`)
This is the lower-level approach:

```python
from starlette.types import ASGIApp, Receive, Scope, Send

class AuthMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, app: ASGIApp):
        self.app = app

    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send):
        if scope["type"] == "http":
            # your auth logic here
            token = dict(scope.get("headers", [])).get(b"authorization", b"").decode()
            if not token:
                # reject request
                pass
        await self.app(scope, receive, send)
```

### 2. BaseHTTPMiddleware (using `dispatch`)
This is the higher-level, easier approach:

```python
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from starlette.requests import Request

class AuthMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        token = request.headers.get("authorization")
        if not token:
            return Response("Unauthorized", status_code=401)
        response = await call_next(request)
        return response
```

## When to use which?
- Use `dispatch` (BaseHTTPMiddleware) → simpler, cleaner, recommended for most use cases
- Use `__call__` (Pure ASGI) → better performance, needed for WebSockets or streaming

## Register in FastAPI:
```python
app.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware)
```

Hope this helps! 🚀

ISSUE #14454: OAuth2 security schemes duplicated in OpenAPI, with and without scopes, when used at the router level
Author: tiangolo
Date: 2025-12-04T12:35:06Z
Labels: bug
State: closed

[c0]
### Privileged issue

- [x] I'm @tiangolo or he asked me directly to create an issue here.

### Issue Content

OAuth2 security schemes duplicated in OpenAPI, with and without scopes, when used at the router level

Reported by @Kludex on another channel 🙌 

(I'm working on it)

```Python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#   "fastapi[standard]==0.121.3",
# ]
# ///

import json
import sys
from typing import Annotated

import fastapi
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, FastAPI, Security
from fastapi.security import OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer, SecurityScopes


# print the dependencies
print(f'fastapi version = {fastapi.__version__}')
print(f'Python version = {sys.version}')



app = FastAPI()

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer(
    authorizationUrl='api/oauth/authorize',
    tokenUrl='/api/oauth/token',
    refreshUrl='/api/oauth/token',
    auto_error=False,
    scopes={'read': 'Read access', 'write': 'Write access'},
)

async def get_token(
    token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)],
) -> str:
    return token

AccessToken = Annotated[str, Depends(get_token, use_cache=True)]


async def require_oauth_scopes(security_scopes: SecurityScopes, token: AccessToken) -> None:
    pass        


async def check_limit(token: AccessToken) -> None:
    pass

# The problem is here. If we remove the dependency from the router, the schema is generated correctly in both fastapi versions.
router = APIRouter(prefix='/v1', dependencies=[Depends(check_limit)])

channels_router = APIRouter(prefix='/channels', tags=['Channels'])
@channels_router.get("/", dependencies=[Security(require_oauth_scopes, scopes=['read'])])
def read_items():
    return {"msg": "You have READ access"}


router.include_router(channels_router)

app.include_router(router)
schema = app.openapi()
pretty_schema = json.dumps(schema, indent=4)
print(pretty_schema)

"""
with fastapi 0.123.7, the generated openapi schema icludes security without scopes:

                "security": [
                    {
                        "OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer": []
                    }
                ]

but in fastapi 0.121.3, the generated openapi schema includes two items in security:

                "security": [
                    {
                        "OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer": []
                    },
                    {
                        "OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer": [
                            "read"
                        ]
                    }
                ]
"""
```

title: APIKeyBase interface changed since version 0.122.0 and not mentioned in changelog.
need_summary: The developer needed to know that FastAPI 0.122 changed the APIKeyBase constructor, breaking custom API key security schemes, and must update the subclass accordingly; the answer cites version 0.122 and provides a concrete code fix.
security_topic: breaking change in FastAPI APIKeyBase constructor affecting custom security scheme
question_text: Previously `ApiKeyBase` doesn't have constructor method, now it has and it will not only require some positional arguments but overrides class property `model`. I think it's worth mentioning in changelog because it's breaking change - all arguments of constructor are not optional.
answer_text:
just ran into this upgrading from 0.121 to 0.122. completely broke our custom API key security scheme.

pre-0.122:
```python
class CustomAPIKey(APIKeyBase):
    pass  # just worked
```

post-0.122 you need to pass the required args:
```python
class CustomAPIKey(APIKeyBase):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(
            name="X-API-Key",
            scheme_name="CustomAPIKey",
            description="Custom API key auth",
        )
```

[c0]


### Issue Content

We have found at least 2 regression in the way forms are handled while trying to migrate to v0.115.11 from version v0.112.4. index 6083b731..db7eedba 100644
--- a/fastapi/dependencies/utils.py
+++ b/fastapi/dependencies/utils.py
@@ -789,9 +789,9 @@ async def _extract_form_body(

-    for key, value in received_body.items():

+    # for key, value in received_body.items():

title: Basic auth `realm` is REQUIRED but handled as optional
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether the `realm` parameter in HTTP Basic auth is required by the spec, and the answer cites RFC 7617 and RFC 7235 (including Appendix A) showing that the realm is now optional.
security_topic: requirement of realm parameter for HTTP Basic authentication
question_text: According to https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 , specification of the `realm` parameter is REQUIRED, so making `realm` optional here https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/643d2845de09a437b955a163ab25eb0887bfd0e1/fastapi/security/http.py#L195 and at related places, is misleading and makes it easy to create non-conforming APIs. It bit me when a Shelly device refused (rightfully) to authenticate against the API which was using the default (missing) `realm` behavior.
answer_text:
I think we should close this issue.

As Sebastian mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/13786#pullrequestreview-3501695067), `realm` seems to be not required in latest version of RFC.

> I also noted that the spec says that the realm is now optional, but only in a footer note (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A). 😂 Anyway, we are good with that now.

I checked this and agree:

The https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 states:

> The authentication parameter 'realm' is REQUIRED ([RFC7235], Section 2.2).

But if we go to Section 2.2 of RFC7235, we have:

> [2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2.2).  Protection Space (Realm)
>    The "realm" authentication parameter is reserved for use by
>    authentication schemes that wish to indicate a scope of protection.
>    A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme
>    and authority components of the effective request URI; see [Section](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)
>    [5.5 of [RFC7230]](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)) of the server being accessed, **in combination with**
>    **the realm value if present.** ...

So, current version of RFC7235 doesn't say that `realm` is required.

Moreover, it's mentioned in [Appendix A](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A):

>    The "realm" parameter is no longer always required on challenges;
>    consequently, the ABNF allows challenges without any auth parameters.
>    ([Section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2))

and at related places, is misleading and makes it easy to create non-conforming APIs. It bit me when a Shelly device refused (rightfully) to authenticate against the API which was using the default (missing) `realm` behavior.

comments.author: tvogel
comments.body: Ah, good that this is already in the works! However, the fix to default it to "global" is questionable to me because that is a string that in general gets presented to users as a prompt to provide credentials, so shouldn't have a rather meaningless default. A good framework should make the framework user provide relevant detail like the realm. If they use basic auth, they need to define a realm.

comments.author: YuriiMotov
comments.body:
I think we should close this issue.

As Sebastian mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/13786#pullrequestreview-3501695067), `realm` seems to be not required in latest version of RFC.

> I also noted that the spec says that the realm is now optional, but only in a footer note (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A). 😂 Anyway, we are good with that now.


I checked this and agree:

The https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 states:

> The authentication parameter 'realm' is REQUIRED ([RFC7235], Section 2.2).

But if we go to Section 2.2 of RFC7235, we have:

> [2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2.2).  Protection Space (Realm)
> 
>    The "realm" authentication parameter is reserved for use by
>    authentication schemes that wish to indicate a scope of protection.
> 
>    A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme
>    and authority components of the effective request URI; see [Section](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)
>    [5.5 of [RFC7230]](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)) of the server being accessed, **in combination with**
>    **the realm value if present.** ...

So, current version of RFC7235 doesn't say that `realm` is required.

Moreover, it's mentioned in [Appendix A](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A):

>    The "realm" parameter is no longer always required on challenges;
>    consequently, the ABNF allows challenges without any auth parameters.
>    ([Section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2))
