title: Basic auth accepts wrong password as a correct one!
need_summary: The developer asked if FastAPI’s HTTPBasic auth was incorrectly accepting any password because the Swagger UI “Authorize” button bypasses verification, and the maintainer replied that the button does not perform verification and pointed to the FastAPI HTTP Basic Auth documentation (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/http-basic-auth/).
security_topic: Swagger UI Authorize button does not validate credentials
question_text: Hi I'm struggling to place a basic auth, and using the latest fastapi version but still the app is working with any random string
answer_text:
That's not an issue.

On the other side, your code is working as expected, I'm going to assume, that when you said that is working with any random string, you're referring to the swagger green button for "Authorize". Remember, that button has no verification after you enter your credentials. If you run your code without putting anything in Authorize beforehand, you're going to see something like:

![image](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/assets/72013291/2240754d-7ff9-4c53-b43c-c5a651bdd7e8)

And that input has the verification of your code to check username and password.

Check this for more info: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/http-basic-auth/

title: HTTPBearer security scheme is returning 403 instead or 401
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether FastAPI's HTTPBearer should return a 401 or 403 for missing or malformed Authorization headers, and the answer cites RFC 6750 (Section 3.1) indicating that 401 is the appropriate status code.
security_topic: appropriate HTTP status code for unauthenticated bearer token requests
question_text: Hey @Kludex, what do you think about raising a `HTTP 400 BAD REQUEST` for cases where the authentication scheme is not correctly 'bearer'?
answer_text:
Sorry, my misunderstanding. At any rate, I don't think it is necessary after reading section 3 again I realised they offered an example for this scenario.

**tldr; 401 seems like the appropriate error code 👍** 

```
 If the request lacks any authentication information (e.g., the client
   was unaware that authentication is necessary or attempted using an
   unsupported authentication method), the resource server SHOULD NOT
   include an error code or other error information.

   For example:

     HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
     WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example"
```
thread_text:
ISSUE #10177: HTTPBearer security scheme is returning 403 instead or 401 Author: Kludex Date: 2023-08-31T06:26:52Z Labels: bug State: closed [c0] ### Discussed in https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/discussions/9130
Originally posted by **aaaaahaaaaa** September 8, 2020 HTTPBearer security scheme enabled as a dependency is returning a `403` when a request is unauthenticated because of a missing or a malformed `authorization` header. In those scenarios, a `401` should be returned instead.
## Related PRs - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/2120 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/5310 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/5332 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/9312 --- COMMENTS --- [c1] @ordinary-jamie 2023-09-12T07:24:52Z: Hey @Kludex, what do you think about raising a `HTTP 400 BAD REQUEST` for cases where the authentication scheme is not correctly 'bearer'? [From RFC 6750 Section 3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750#section-3.1): ``` invalid_request The request is missing a required parameter, includes an unsupported parameter or parameter value, repeats the same parameter, uses more than one method for including an access token, or is otherwise malformed. The resource server SHOULD respond with the HTTP 400 (Bad Request) status code. invalid_token The access token provided is expired, revoked, malformed, or invalid for other reasons. The resource SHOULD respond with the HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) status code. The client MAY request a new access token and retry the protected resource request. ``` My reading of this text is that: - when the server understands the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is correct) but the token itself is malformed we should return a `401` - when the server does **not** understand the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is wrong), then we should return a `400` --- [c2] @ordinary-jamie 2023-09-12T07:29:32Z: [`fastapi/security/http.py` L#125](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/security/http.py#L125-L130) EDIT: Wrong line sorry --- [c3] @ordinary-jamie 2023-09-12T07:59:35Z: Sorry, my misunderstanding. At any rate, I don't think it is necessary after reading section 3 again I realised they offered an example for this scenario. **tldr; 401 seems like the appropriate error code 👍** ``` If the request lacks any authentication information (e.g., the client was unaware that authentication is necessary or attempted using an unsupported authentication method), the resource server SHOULD NOT include an error code or other error information. For example: HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example" ``` --- [c4] @bootrecords 2023-09-13T13:13:06Z: This not only affects the `HTTPBearer`, but a lot of other classes in the `security` scope also return 403 in `"Not authenticated"` cases where they should return 401 instead, such as the `OAuth2` class (though strangely enough not the subclasses `OAuth2PasswordBearer` and `OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer`), the `HTTPBase` class and its sublasses (except for `HTTPBasic` for some reason), all classes in `api_key.py` and `OpenIdConnect`. Would probably be good if that could be straightened out for all occurrences there. --- [c5] @eastack 2025-01-08T05:03:36Z: Will there be any progress in the future? Will this error be fixed? I just hope that when the client receives a 403 response, it prompts the user that they do not have access to the corresponding resource, and when a 401 response is received, it redirects to the login page. It seems that this cannot be achieved with the current default implementation of FastAPI. --- [c6] @asmaier 2025-11-28T15:40:34Z: This change broke some of our tests. As a workaround limit the version to `fastapi[all]<0.122.0"` or fix your tests to expect now 401 instead of 403. --- [c7] @YuriiMotov 2025-11-28T16:40:40Z: > This change broke some of our tests. comments.author: ordinary-jamie
comments.body:
Hey @Kludex, what do you think about raising a `HTTP 400 BAD REQUEST` for cases where the authentication scheme is not correctly 'bearer'?

[From RFC 6750 Section 3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750#section-3.1):

```
invalid_request
         The request is missing a required parameter, includes an
         unsupported parameter or parameter value, repeats the same
         parameter, uses more than one method for including an access
         token, or is otherwise malformed.  The resource server SHOULD
         respond with the HTTP 400 (Bad Request) status code.

invalid_token
         The access token provided is expired, revoked, malformed, or
         invalid for other reasons.  The resource SHOULD respond with
         the HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) status code.  The client MAY
         request a new access token and retry the protected resource
         request.
```

My reading of this text is that:

- when the server understands the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is correct) but the token itself is malformed we should return a `401`
- when the server does **not** understand the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is wrong), then we should return a `400`

DISCUSSION #7176: Client certificate verification (mTLS) in Starlette/FastAPI
Author: kaleming
Date: 2020-10-22T13:09:00Z

[c0]
I have found two discussions about this topic, but no solution using Fastapi was proposed:

- Issue #1029
- [Stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59637254/how-to-do-client-certificate-verification-mtls-in-starlette-fastapi)

According to Starlette documentation, no certificate verification is natively implemented in Starlette. 

[This approach using flask](https://tech-habit.info/posts/https-cert-based-auth-with-flask-and-gunicorn/) to deal with certificate verification works fine. 

It would be very cool if Fastapi support certificate verification.
 

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @Mause 2020-10-23T00:27:38Z:
If you run fastapi with gunicorn with uvicorn workers, the instructions at the bottom of the article you linked will probably fill your need?
---
[c2] @kaleming 2020-10-23T13:03:06Z:
> If you run fastapi with gunicorn with uvicorn workers, the instructions at the bottom of the article you linked will probably fill your need?

Hi @Mause, I will give a try using this approach at the bottom to see if it works fine.
---
[c3] @cryptoroo 2020-11-03T13:39:42Z:
@kaleming  -- this is an interesting one. 

https://www.uvicorn.org/settings/ indicates this is in fact supported however the verification mode will be against the chain rather than more flexibility. 

Looking at the code this is to do with the fact that the Python SSLContext object is not actually exposed (i.e. you can't get the peer (client)) certificate natively. 

For example if you had access to the actual client certificate you could choose a verification strategy. That is the motivation for using L7 (nginx,trafik etc) tools that can put the certificate in the header. 

Saying that this is how I would go about this 

A) You will actually need need two CAs 

- one for creating the Secure SSL channel (think of things like let's encrypt) 
- one for verifying incoming certificates  

B) You will need to choose a Verification mode

- I believe this is related to this flag in uvicorn --ssl-cert-reqs <int> - Whether client certificate is required (see stdlib ssl module's)
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#ssl.CERT_NONE
-  I believe valid values are 0-2 https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#ssl.SSLContext.verify_mode 

C) You will Need to provide your verification CA root and leaf certs

-in a PEM format to pass as this parameter --ssl-ca-certs <str> - CA certificates file

D) If you are developing in a local environment then you will also need to map a hostname to an ip. 
- Let's say your CA Certificate is for bob.alice.xyz you will need to create a mapping for bob.alice.xyz in your local PC dns so that the CA certificate will be trusted and a secure channel can be established
- Most Client SSL and Browsers won't treat a connection as secure unless the hostname requested and the one on cert match. 
- You can disable this behavior for example in postman or HTTP Client libraries. 

Long story short this should be doable however I might need to do some more experimentation.

@kaleming -- i have got MTLS working 👍

That all works fine but how do we get the client info to fastapi ? I checked headers but no success.

I'm looking for the CN of the client certificate to perform authorisation based on that.
---
[c12] @septatrix 2022-01-15T17:15:12Z:
As far as I know this is currently impossible as the ASGI spec does not provide access to any information on the transport level. The current status can be seen in the corresponding issue in the asgiref repo: https://github.com/django/asgiref/issues/112
---
[c13] @stereobutter 2022-10-26T10:13:53Z:
As far as I understand the ASGI spec *extensions* may be used to pass additional information from the server to the application. In fact the ASGI spec seems to already specify an [TLS extension](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/tls.html).

Using the extension would look something like this:

```python
@app.get("/foo")
def foo(request: Request):
    if 'tls' in request.scope.extensions:
        client_name = request.scope.extensions['tls']['client_cert_name']
    ...
```

I don't fully understand how that relates to https://github.com/django/asgiref/issues/112 but to me it appears that at least for TLS/mTLS all the necessary pieces are specified and ASGI servers and applications are free to implement this?

@cryptoroo it's great that you wrote an article! 😎

It seems all this would actually be outside of FastAPI, right? At the server (Uvicorn) level or in users' code, right?

[c3] @caeser1996 2023-02-06T23:49:18Z:
FastAPI doesn't provide built-in support for WebSockets (WSS). However, you can use an external library like websockets to add WebSockets functionality to your FastAPI application. Here's an example of how you can create a WebSockets endpoint in FastAPI using websockets:
```
from fastapi import FastAPI
import websockets

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
async def get():
    return {"message": "Hello, WebSockets"}

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket, path):
    await websocket.send("Hello, client!")
    while True:
        data = await websocket.recv()
        await websocket.send(f"You said: {data}")

```
In this example, a websocket endpoint is created using the websockets library and decorated with the @app.websocket decorator provided by FastAPI. The websocket endpoint takes a websocket object and a path argument and can be used to send and receive messages between the client and the server.

[c1] @moadennagi 2023-01-03T10:44:20Z:
I would use a middleware and plug it when mounting gradio app to fastapi app. Here is an example using starlette.middleware.base

```python
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

from starlette.routing import Mount
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

class CustomHeaderMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        auth_header = request.headers.get('Authorization')
        if not auth_header:
            raise HTTPException(401)
        # Logic for parsing token, getting user ...
        response = await call_next(request)
        return response

subapi = FastAPI()

@subapi.get("/sub/1")
def read_sub():
    return {"message": "Hello World from sub API / 1"}

subapi.get("/sub/2")
def sub2():
    return {"message": "Hello World from sub API / 2"}


middleware = [
    Middleware(CustomHeaderMiddleware)
]

routes = [
    Mount('/subapi', app=subapi, middleware=middleware),
]

app = FastAPI(routes=routes)

@app.get("/app")
def read_main():
    return {"message": "Hello World from main app"}
```

[c2] @moadennagi 2023-01-04T10:26:21Z:
I looked into gradio documentation (https://gradio.app/sharing_your_app/#accessing-the-network-request-directly), gradio provides ability to access the request data on the main function, you can access session cookies, headers ... and do various checks, here is a simplified example:

```python
import gradio as gr
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Response

CUSTOM_PATH = "/gradio"

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
def read_main():
    return {"message": "This is your main app"}

# I added this as a get request to be able to easily set cookie through the browser 
@app.get('/login')
def dummy_login(response: Response):
    response.set_cookie(key='fakesession', value='fake-cookie-session-value')
    return {'message': 'logged in'}

def echo(name, request: gr.Request):
    if request:
        try:
            getattr(request.cookies, 'fakesession')
            # do some checks and validations ...
        except AttributeError:
            raise HTTPException(401, detail='Must be logged in')
        return "Hello, " + name + "!"
    return name

io = gr.Interface(echo, "textbox", "textbox")
app = gr.mount_gradio_app(app, io, path=CUSTOM_PATH)

```
This other example uses middleware to run before all requests to gradio path:
```python
import gradio as gr

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

CUSTOM_PATH = "/gradio"

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
def read_main():
    return {"message": "This is your main app"}

@app.middleware('http')
async def auth(request: Request, call_next):
    if request.scope['path'].startswith(CUSTOM_PATH):
        # do some auth checks ...
        print('checks')
        pass
    response = await call_next(request)
    return response

io = gr.Interface(lambda x: "hi" + x, "textbox", "textbox")
app = gr.mount_gradio_app(app, io, path=CUSTOM_PATH)
```
I'm not sure using `startswith` is the best option as it would cover all paths starting with gradio (gradio/... but also gradiosometext), you could me refine that using regex.

title: TrustedHostMiddleware ignores port in Host header
need_summary: The developer asked if TrustedHostMiddleware should consider the port in the Host header, and the answer references the Starlette middleware source line (https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/master/starlette/middleware/trustedhost.py#L38) and RFC 9110 host header specification.
security_topic: host header validation and port handling in TrustedHostMiddleware
question_text: Using the provided example code and making a request from localhost:8000 I get an "Invalid host header" response, even though looking at dev tools in chrome the header is `Host: localhost:8000`. If I change to `allowed_hosts=["localhost"]` it works fine. I understand it's a trusted host, and not a trusted port, but seems strange to me that it says invalid host header even though thats exactly what the browser is sending in the host header. Not sure if this is intended behaviour or not.
answer_text:
The port should be specified when you want to run the server, not on the allowed hosts.

```python
uvicorn.run(
        "backend.apps.core.main:server", host="0.0.0.0", port=3000, reload=True
    )
```

As you can see https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/#trustedhostmiddleware, the allowed hosts (without their port numbers) are been specified. The port that you passed to uvicorn is where you'll be able to access your allowed hosts from.

With that said, as long as you use the above port (3000), you should be able to access the domain names, given that your proxy or whatever server you are using defaults to the port.

A hostname is the name of a server, which resolve to one (or multiple) IP addresses. You should not include the port as it have nothing do with hostname.

> @iudeen @aybruhm 
> I understand that, but the Host header is passed with a port from the browser, and the TrustedHostMiddleware works on the basis of that header.

The port should be specified when you want to run the server, not on the allowed hosts. 

`uvicorn.run(
        "backend.apps.core.main:server", host="0.0.0.0", port=3000, reload=True
    )`

With that said, as long as you use the above port (3000), you should be able to access the domain names, given that your proxy or whatever server you are using defaults to the port.

title: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' error when redirecting the frontend
need_summary: The developer needed guidance on fixing the CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin error when using FastAPI's RedirectResponse, and the answer advised adding the necessary headers manually and referenced the MDN CORS documentation and Starlette's RedirectResponse source code.
security_topic: CORS handling for redirect responses
question_text: I have a FastAPI backend (port: 8000) and NextJs frontend (port: 3000) and from the frontend I am sending a put request which inserts user data into a user's object, and after it is done send a redirection response to `http://localhost:3000/test` (redirect to a frontend path), but it is not doing so and giving CORS No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' error.
answer_text: @tempcoderr I think `RedirectResponse` doesn't return a `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` response header. I read the `RedirectResponse` implementation of `starlette`. It doesn't contain the `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` header. I think you should add these headers by yourself. About the CORS, you can refer to this link (https://developer.mozilla.org/zh-CN/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS). And `RedirectResponse` also has a keyword argument -- `header=...`, you can see the starlette's docs and source code.

}

### Description

Hi.  I'm creating a protected API service that is mounted at `/api` with `uvicorn --root-path /api`.  It is protected with `OAuth2PasswordBearer`, as described in [FastAPI Security Tutorial](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/security/).  However, `tokenUrl` in `openapi.json` does not respect `root_path`.  When I'm working on my local development server without `--root-path /api`, `tokenUrl` in `openapi.json` is `/token`.  When it is deployed onto my server with `--root-path /api`, it is still `/token`, where it should be `/api/token`.  As a result, the Swagger UI log in always fails.

Currently I did a dirty fix in the `custom_openapi` function:

    def custom_openapi()
        if app.openapi_schema:
            return app.openapi_schema
        openapi_schema = get_openapi()
        if "servers" in openapi_schema:
            root_path: str = openapi_schema["servers"][0]["url"]
            openapi_schema["components"]["securitySchemes"][
                "OAuth2PasswordBearer"]["flows"]["password"]["tokenUrl"] \
                = root_path + openapi_schema["components"]["securitySchemes"][
                "OAuth2PasswordBearer"]["flows"]["password"]["tokenUrl"]
        app.openapi_schema = openapi_schema
        return app.openapi_schema
    
    app: FastAPI = FastAPI()
    app.openapi = custom_openapi

But this does not work if I have multiple servers in the future.

How can I make `tokenUrl` to respect the current `root_path`?  Did I missed something?

title: Header 'Date' ignored inside request headers
need_summary: The developer needed to know that the `Date` header is a forbidden header in the Fetch API and therefore cannot be sent via Swagger UI, as documented on MDN (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Date) and the XMLHttpRequest specification.
security_topic: Forbidden HTTP header handling in Swagger UI
question_text: Do you have any solution to include and read date header???
answer_text:
You can't. Since you are sending a request it MUST be terminated according to the standard when you set a whole list of prohibited headers:

https://www.w3.org/TR/2010/CR-XMLHttpRequest-20100803/

Terminate these steps if header is a case‑insensitive match for one of the following headers:

- Accept-Charset
- Accept-Encoding
- Connection
- Content-Length
- Cookie
- Cookie2
- Content-Transfer-Encoding
- Date
- Expect
- Host
- Keep-Alive
- Referer
- TE
- Trailer
- Transfer-Encoding
- Upgrade
- User-Agent
- Via

title: Using scopes on `Security()` changes dependency inheritance
need_summary: The developer asked why adding scopes to Security() changes dependency inheritance resulting in different Session objects, and the maintainer explained that FastAPI includes security scopes in the dependency cache key, citing the Dependant class source line and the FastAPI documentation on dependency caching and OAuth2 scopes.
security_topic: dependency cache behavior with security scopes
question_text: I'm wondering if this has anything to do with the instantiation of a SecurityScopes at some point by Security().
answer_text:
[Dependant](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L15) object has a cache_key attribute which the dependency resolver of fastapi uses it to cache dependencies and use the already resolved dependencies (get_session in this case).
according to [this line](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L58) of Dependant class the cache_key is generated using the **dependency function reference** and **security scopes**.
when you use get_authenticated_user as a security dependency every param in get_authenticated_user gets the security scopes of the parent api (user_activate).
so when resloving dependencies from user_activate with scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ('activate'))```
when resloving dependencies from user_activate with no scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ())```

i think this behavior might be a security feature.

it might help you to read [this part of the doc](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/?h=dependenc#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times) on dependency cache
and [this part](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes/?h=dependency#dependency-tree-and-scopes) about dependency tree and scopes.

title: Question: How can we setup AD authentication?
need_summary: The developer needed guidance on configuring Active Directory authentication in FastAPI, and the answer provided a concrete example using the ldap3 library (https://pypi.org/project/ldap3/) with FastAPI SessionMiddleware as a cited source.
security_topic: Active Directory authentication integration for FastAPI
question_text: How can we setup AD authentication?
answer_text:
@Bahu2016 you could probably use an external library like https://pypi.org/project/ldap3/
To use the `ldap3 `library to set up AD integration in FastAPI, you can use the `Connection `and `Server `classes to establish a connection to the AD server and authenticate users.
In this example, the `Server `class is used to create a server instance for the AD server, and the `Connection `class is used to establish a connection and authenticate the user. The user and password parameters are used to specify the username and password for the user to authenticate. If the authentication is successful, the bind method will return True, otherwise it will return False.

After a user successfully logs in to your FastAPI application, you may want to keep track of their session to store information about the user, such as their username, permissions, and preferences. This can be useful for implementing features such as user authentication and authorization, and for maintaining user-specific state in your application.

To keep a session in FastAPI, you can use the SessionMiddleware provided by the fastapi module. This middleware uses cookies to store session data, and it provides methods for accessing and modifying the session data.

Here is an example of how to use ldap3 & SessionMiddleware in FastAPI: (untested, because i don't have an AD)

```py
from fastapi import FastAPI, SessionMiddleware
from ldap3 import Connection, Server

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(SessionMiddleware, secret_key="ChangeY0urS3creT!")

@app.on_event("startup")
async def startup():
    global ad_server
    ad_server = Server("ad.example.com", port=389, use_ssl=False)

@app.post("/login")
async def login(request, username: str, password: str):
    conn = Connection(ad_server, user=username, password=password)
    if conn.bind():
        # Store the user's username in the session
        request.session["username"] = username
        # Store the user's name and email in the session
        user = conn.search(f"cn={username}", attributes=["givenName", "mail"])
        request.session["name"] = user["givenName"]
        request.session["email"] = user["mail"]
        # Store the user's groups in the session
        groups = conn.search(f"cn={username}", attributes=["memberOf"])
        request.session["groups"] = groups["memberOf"]

title: How we can manage roles and permissions using fast-API dynamically?
need_summary: The developer needed guidance on dynamically managing roles and permissions (authorization) in FastAPI, answered by referencing the FastAPI OAuth2 scopes documentation (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes).
security_topic: dynamic role and permission management in FastAPI
question_text: I research a lot but not find any good way to manage roles and permission dynamically using FastApi. if you guys have any idea please let me know.Thanks in  advance
answer_text:
Can you please clarify what is wrong with the code snippet and what you are trying to accomplish, as well as what you mean by managing roles and permissions dynamically?

There is a section in the documentation about using oauth2.0 scopes (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes) which is a way to manage permissions. As mentioned in the docs, you will want to have some way to persist the permissions for each user (using a database of some sort or using a predefined list of permissions).

You can also create a custom dependency to check permissions each time the user makes a request to your endpoints, which may be necessary if you need the ability to immediately revoke permissions for a user without invalidating their JWT.

title: Obtain SSL client certificate from FastAPI request
need_summary: How to retrieve the distinguished name from an SSL client certificate in FastAPI, answered with a monkey‑patch using uvicorn's HttpToolsProtocol and accessing the SSL object via request.scope['transport'].get_extra_info('ssl_object').getpeercert()['subject'] (see uvicorn issue #400).
security_topic: retrieving client SSL certificate details in FastAPI
question_text: how do I obtain the DN from the SSL client cert?
answer_text:
I've made some progress. Reading this:

https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/issues/400

I assume the issue sits with uvicorn, not exposing the cert. This monkeypatch works:

```
from uvicorn.protocols.http.httptools_impl import HttpToolsProtocol
old_on_url = HttpToolsProtocol.on_url
def new_on_url(self,url):
    old_on_url(self, url)
    self.scope['transport'] = self.transport
HttpToolsProtocol.on_url = new_on_url
```

Which allows the subject DN to be retrieved as follows:

```
@app.get("/")
async def get_root(request:Request):
  t= request.scope["transport"].get_extra_info("ssl_object").getpeercert()["subject"]
```

and t is a tuple of data, which is a litltle tedious to parse but better than nothing.

It's both a brilliant and horrible hack - is there a better way? :)

title: "request.json()" hangs indefinitely in middleware
need_summary: How to read the request body for security-related processing (e.g., HMAC validation) without hanging, answered by using FastAPI dependencies as a workaround (see FastAPI issue #394 and the FastAPI dependencies documentation).
security_topic: reading request body in middleware for security validation without blocking
question_text: I need to read the body in JSON format in several middleware in order to process the data for various reasons (logging, security, sanitizing, etc.) so I wonder what the correct implementation would be in order to avoid halting the program?
answer_text:
@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```

thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

Is it possible to stream a request multiple times in FastAPI using `self.stream()`? I tried various approches, like copying the `Request` object, but none of them worked.
---
[c7] @xingdongzhe 2022-10-05T14:47:17Z:
@araujo88 It can't be using `self.stream()`, for per request, only one time can use `self.stream()`.  
Or you will hang forever because of `await self.event_message.wait()`  
[You can see here: uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fedf67e68d3f81c846bf3740c8ae21fa133000a4/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543)  
This is because that when `self.stream()` done, there are no action to notify `self.event_message`
This `asyncio.Event` will be notified of four actions:
- when Connection Lost
- when body_data received
- when body_data readed done
- when write reponse data done

```

    print(chunk)
await request.json()
```

@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

title: Cookies Received, but doesn't stored inside the browser
need_summary: The developer needed to know why the Secure and SameSite cookie settings prevented the browser from storing the cookie, and the answer referenced the MDN documentation that SameSite=None requires Secure and suggested using SameSite=Lax with Secure=False.
security_topic: Cookie not stored due to SameSite and Secure flag settings
question_text: tldr; get responses back from cookies, but it doesn't stored on the application, and still able to send it on every request.
answer_text:
I guess that he meant that yellow warning sign.
If you use `SameSite=none`, it is required to set `secure` attribute aswell as described here https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite.
This error is about that.
But you can still use `SameSite=Lax` (with `secure=False`) and it **should** work.
```py3
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/home")
def home(response: Response):
    response.set_cookie(key="foo", value="bar", secure=False, samesite="lax")
    return {"foo": "bar"}
```

comments.body:
I guess that he meant that yellow warning sign.
If you use `SameSite=none`, it is required to set `secure` attribute aswell as described [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite).
This error is about that.
But you can still use `SameSite=Lax` (with `secure=False`) and it **should** work.
```py3
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/home")
def home(response: Response):
    response.set_cookie(key="foo", value="bar", secure=False, samesite="lax")
    return {"foo": "bar"}

title: CORS middleware not working !
need_summary: The developer needed to know that CORS middleware cannot be configured with allow_origins=['*'] and allow_credentials=True simultaneously, as documented in the FastAPI CORS tutorial (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/#use-corsmiddleware).
security_topic: CORS middleware does not apply to 500 Internal Server Error responses
question_text: When I make a request from Frontend with axios and whenever I made a request, it is showing the CORS error. And I already have setup the CORS middleware in fastapi.
answer_text: Yeah this is a common misconception about the CORS middleware: it doesn't work on HTTP 500 response codes. There are several discussions on it in this repo and also in Starlette (where this was actually decided on). So, look in your server logs for the reason of the 500 Internal Server Error and ignore the CORS.

title: response cookie values need use 'utf-8' encode
need_summary: The developer needed to know why FastAPI/Starlette encodes cookie values with latin-1 and where to change this behavior, which the maintainer answered by citing RFC 7230's requirement for latin-1 encoding.
security_topic: Set-Cookie header encoding requirement (latin-1) per RFC
question_text:
i found it had been hard code in the method

or where can i change it?
answer_text:
This is not a FastAPI issue, but a Starlette implementation.

But in regards to your question, the RFC 7230 requires that it is encoded with latin-1, and they follow that specification. Chances are small they will change this any time soon, so either make sure your headers are latin-1 encodable or make your own version of Starlette with this change in it.

question_text: I am running standard FastAPI with CORS middleware. I noticed that a trailing backslash at the URL makes a 307 Temporary Redirect. It is fine when you have an http URL. But it is not working as expected when you have a HTTPS URL. It replaces HTTPS with HTTP.

   return responses.PlainTextResponse("Example")

```
uvicorn server:app --host 192.168.1.79 --port 8001

curl -I -H "X-Forwarded-Proto: https" -H "Host: blah.com" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 169.255.255.1" 192.168.1.79:8001/path
HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
date: Thu, 19 Jan 2023 10:39:23 GMT
server: uvicorn

3) And the documentation says you need to include `--forwarded-allow-ips='*'`

```

HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
date: Thu, 19 Jan 2023 10:39:23 GMT
server: uvicorn
location: https://blah.com/path/
```

Perhaps this could be made more obvious in the documentation somewhere?

Also, you should limit `--forwarded-allow-ips` to the address of your proxy only

title: jsonable_encoder alters json_encoders of Pydantic objects
need_summary: The developer needed to know why jsonable_encoder mutates the Pydantic model’s json_encoders causing secret values to be exposed, and the answer provides a concrete fix by merging encoders with `{**encoder, **custom_encoder}` anchored in commit 39cc2925 (see the diff).
security_topic: global encoder mutation causing secret value leakage
question_text: My understanding is that passing `custom_encoder` should only affect the current call and not modify any global state.
answer_text:
Yes, copying `encoder` before modifying it fixes the issue. Since FastAPI requires at least Python 3.6 merging the dictionaries could also be done with `{**a, **b}`, so an alternative fix would look like this:

```diff
diff --git a/fastapi/encoders.py b/fastapi/encoders.py
index 4b7ffe31..39cc2925 100644
--- a/fastapi/encoders.py
+++ b/fastapi/encoders.py
@@ -52,7 +52,7 @@ def jsonable_encoder(
     if isinstance(obj, BaseModel):
         encoder = getattr(obj.__config__, "json_encoders", {})
         if custom_encoder:
-            encoder.update(custom_encoder)
+            encoder = {**encoder, **custom_encoder}
         obj_dict = obj.dict(
             include=include,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
             exclude=exclude,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
``` 

Note that I'm not sure yet if the change has any negative side effects. Would be good to know to know if there was a reason why `.update()` was used in the first place. :thinking:

title: default HTTPException handler adds content when there should be none
need_summary: The developer needed to know that FastAPI’s default HTTPException handler always returns a JSON body even for status codes like 304/204, which may lead to unintended data exposure, and the maintainer referenced the handler implementation in the FastAPI source (see fastapi/exception_handlers.py lines 9‑16) as the concrete anchor.
security_topic: default HTTPException handler returns body for 304/204 responses
question_text: This appears to be an issue where the default FastAPI handler for HTTPExceptions always returns content even for status codes (304, 204), where no content should be specified.
answer_text:
The default handler for HTTPException will always construct a JSONResponse with content. https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/22528373bba6a654323de416ad5c867cbadb81bb/fastapi/exception_handlers.py#L9-L16

This behavior is documented in the tip here: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/#the-resulting-response

This is incompatible with returning HTTP status codes that shouldn't have any content. Whether or not fastapi should choose whether to send a JSONResponse or not based on the status code is debatable, but since this behavior isn't implemented today, you can build it with your own exception handler. If you have to use exceptions instead of returning the response directly, some sample code would be:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from starlette.requests import Request

app = FastAPI()

Hi,

The default handler for HTTPException will always construct a JSONResponse with content. https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/22528373bba6a654323de416ad5c867cbadb81bb/fastapi/exception_handlers.py#L9-L16

This is incompatible with returning HTTP status codes that shouldn't have any content. Whether or not fastapi should choose whether to send a JSONResponse or not based on the status code is debatable, but since this behavior isn't implemented today, you can build it with your own exception handler. from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from starlette.requests import Request

app = FastAPI()

async def not_modified_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: NotModifiedException):
    return Response(status_code=304)

async def route(request: Request):
    raise NotModifiedException()

```

BTW I prefer a more generic handler
```python
@app.exception_handler(HTTPException)
async def ret(request: Request, exc: HTTPException) -> Response:
    # fastapi's default event handler is bugged (https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/4946)
    headers = getattr(exc, "headers", None)
    if exc.status_code in {204, 304}:
        if headers:
            return Response(status_code=exc.status_code, headers=headers)
        else:
            return Response(status_code=exc.status_code)
    if headers:
        return JSONResponse(
            {"detail": exc.detail}, status_code=exc.status_code, headers=headers
        )
    else:
        return JSONResponse({"detail": exc.detail}, status_code=exc.status_code)
```

title: Testing with oath authentication
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to include a Bearer token in FastAPI test client requests for OAuth2 authentication, and the answer points to the FastAPI testing documentation (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/testing/ and https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-dependencies/).
security_topic: testing OAuth2 authentication in FastAPI
question_text: when I try to run the tests **in a different folder and file**, the authentication fails, ie i get a 401 response.
answer_text:
Is your intention to run `test_foo` with pytest?

You cannot just toss a Depends in there and expect it to work. When you use `Depends` FastAPI knows what to do with it but pytest does not. To pytest you are just setting a default parameter.

You have to authenticate with the test client as an api consumer would (sorta like [here](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/testing/?h=testing#extended-testing-file) ) or override the dependency like [here](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-dependencies/?h=over).

```python
def test_get_endpoint_list():
    response = client.get("/", headers={

    assert response.json() == {"Available Endpoints": ENDPOINT_LIST}

title: Do we solely rely on memory management to call UploadFile.close?
need_summary: The developer needed to know if FastAPI automatically closes UploadFile objects or if manual .close() is required to prevent resource exhaustion, answered with a reference to the FastAPI routing code where files are opened (https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/146f57b8f70c5757dc20edc716dba1b96936a8d6/fastapi/routing.py#L192).
security_topic: potential file descriptor/resource leak in FastAPI UploadFile handling
question_text:
I am uploading a huge file (~1gb). Since all of this is using `SpooledTemporaryFile` internally, the upload should be written to disk right away. Usually in Python, once you are done processing, you would call `close()` on that file. This in turn would free up the disk space used.

Now I can't find any place where this `.close()` is called. Is that right?

If there is no such place, the `close()` is probably called somewhere implicitly? Is it in memory management?

I guess my question is: where is the space (in memory or on disk) freed?
answer_text:
I don't think it's that simple for FastAPI: the files are opened before the request handler is called, and unrelated error, like deseralizing another form field, could cause an exception so that you never even have the opportunity to close the file.

Opened here: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/146f57b8f70c5757dc20edc716dba1b96936a8d6/fastapi/routing.py#L192

But it's totally possible that your request handler never gets called so you'd have no chance to close the file manually

title: Securing routes with Firebase Auth access token
need_summary: The developer needed to know that FastAPI's HTTPBearer automatically rejects requests without a token (403) and that to programmatically enable/disable it they must customize or subclass the HTTPBearer class, as demonstrated in the FastAPI source code at https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/security/http.py#L100.
security_topic: disabling bearer authentication programmatically in FastAPI
question_text:
One more question: Is there any way to computationally turn Bearer auth on/off?

I tried to do it inside the authentication methods, but if no token is passed, a `403 error` is returned before these are even executed.
answer_text:
The code that runs the HTTPBearer is here https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/security/http.py#L100

You can see it will throw a 403 if you do not include the token.

As such using the HTTPBearer probably would not allow you to computationally turn it on and off.

You could take that class and subclass it or make your own that does have some ability to enable or disable it.

### Description

### Prior work & resources
From what I read in the fastAPI docs and tutorials, security is implemented using dependency injections and there are some examples on how to do this where the fastAPI server is both the resource as well as the authentication server.

In Issue #12 I found a mention of the `OAuthFlowImplicit` class, which seems about right for my use case. However I do not have enough background knowledge with the involved libraries to solve the issue on my own, so here is my question:

### My task
I have a frontend that authenticates with firebase auth and receives an bearer token. This token is then sent to the backend in which for certain routes I want to check for both authentication and authorization.

So first I need to extract the token from the header and check if it belongs to a valid user, which can be done using the firebase_admin library:
```
firebase_auth.verify_id_token(access_token)
```

Then I need to get the custom claims and search compare them with a list of authorized claims:
```
firebase_admin.auth.UserRecord.custom_claims.any(...)
```

How do I create appropriate dependency injection functions in order to perform these checks?

I added some firebase implementation to it and came up with the following:
```python
security = HTTPBearer()

api = FastAPI()
security = HTTPBearer()

firebase_client = FirebaseClient(
    firebase_admin_credentials_url=firebase_test_admin_credentials_url
    # ...
)

user_roles = [test_role]

async def firebase_authentication(token: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> dict:
    user = firebase_client.verify_token(token.credentials)
    return user

async def firebase_authorization(user: dict = Depends(firebase_authentication)):
    roles = firebase_client.get_user_roles(user)

    for role in roles:
        if role in user_roles:
            return user

    raise HTTPException(detail="User does not have the required roles", status_code=HTTPStatus.FORBIDDEN)

@api.get("/")
async def root(uid: str = Depends(firebase_authorization)):
    return {"message": "Successfully authenticated & authorized!"}
```

Using a http client like postman, this seems to work perfectly, however when trying it out using the OpenApi docs I noticed that a `403 error` is correctly returned, since **no token is passed in the header**.

It seems like the OpenApi docs does not know about the required header. Is there a way to configure `HTTPBearer` in such a way that this information is inferred?

comments.body:
Can't you just include the header in your tests?

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

router = APIRouter()

security = HTTPBearer()


async def validate_firebase_token(token: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> None:
    ...


@router.get("/", dependencies=[Depends(validate_firebase_token)])
def endpoint() -> None:
    ...



def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


from fastapi.testclient import TestClient


def test_endpoint() -> None:

    test_token = "foo"
    
    async def validate_fake_token(token: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> None:
        assert token.credentials == test_token

    app = create_app()
    app.dependency_overrides[validate_firebase_token] = validate_fake_token

    client = TestClient(app)

    resp = client.get("/", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {test_token}"})
    assert resp.status_code == 200


test_endpoint()
```
